We have ten minutes and two options on the table. Which one, and why?
Option B. It costs significantly less margin, and it pays back twice as fast.
But Option A has the bigger upside. Twice as much volume.
True. But the volume gain does not outweigh the margin cost. A costs almost two points, and B costs less than half a point.
And the downside of B?
Only a third of our customers use the app, so the reach is smaller. And there is some cannibalization.
What is your fallback if B does not work?
We run Option A in one region, head-to-head with B, and we decide in ninety days.
I would choose Option B, and here is why.
It costs significantly less margin than Option A.

Before we vote, let me put the three options side by side, because the numbers are closer than they look. Option one, the broad price cut, has the biggest upside on volume, but it is also by far the most expensive: almost two points of margin. Option two, the loyalty price, is much cheaper, and it pays back in about four months, which is more than twice as fast as option one. Its weakness is reach. Only a third of our customers use the app. Option three, doing nothing, is the cheapest option today and the most expensive one in six months, because our main competitor is already lower on forty of our top items. So my recommendation is option two, with option one as the fallback in one region. And please, nobody call the difference between them negligible. It is about one and a half points of margin.

In a case discussion at a school like Booth, the professor will often ask you to choose between two options and defend your choice in under a minute. Most people compare everything, and the answer gets longer and weaker with every sentence. A stronger answer does three things. First, it starts with the choice: I would choose option B. Second, it compares on one or two dimensions only, the ones that matter most, and it gives the size of the difference. Not cheaper, but significantly cheaper. Not faster, but twice as fast. Third, it names the biggest downside of its own option before anybody else does. That last step is the one that builds trust. A person who can say what is weak in his own recommendation sounds like someone who has already done the analysis, not someone who is selling.
